sources.entry: Senior Engineers are Living in the Future

summary.title: Senior Engineers are Living in the Future
summary.one_liner: Senior engineers appear to be "ahead of the curve" mainly because they get earlier access to information flows, and you can build that same advantage by sharing what you learn.
keywords: why senior engineers seem like wizards
how to grow into a senior engineer
stop comparing yourself to others engineering
takeaways: Senior engineers often seem to be a step ahead because they hear about problems, solutions, and changes earlier than others.
Seniority brings more time for gathering and synthesizing information and more interaction with peers in other teams.
Career advancement and better information access reinforce each other in a positive-feedback loop.
Avoid comparing yourself with more senior colleagues; first meet your manager's expectations for development work.
Improve your team's value by sharing the information you have access to and showing junior members what is happening behind the scenes.
summary.summary: Zane Bitter's essay uses a thought experiment about a time traveller coworker from a year in the future to frame why senior engineers seem to always have the answers. He argues the effect comes from structural advantages: seniors are asked for help first, hear about projects and management changes earlier, and interact more across teams. He describes the resulting seniority feedback loop and gives advice to stop comparing yourself to others, meet team expectations, and share visibility with junior members. The piece is a reflective essay rather than a technical tutorial.
